hero.body:
Port St. Lucie residents will pay more for trash service after the City Council approved an increase to the annual solid waste assessment Monday night. The council approved Resolution 26-R70, raising the annual assessment by $14.83 per dwelling unit, from $467.33 to $482.16 for the fiscal year beginning in October. There was no public comment or council discussion before the item was read and approved.

The assessment pays for garbage collection, disposal services, facilities and related solid waste programs. It is collected through residents' property tax bills. The increase amounts to about $1.24 more per month for residential properties.

City officials previously said the increase is required under Port St. Lucie's solid waste franchise agreement with FCC Environmental Service and reflects rising costs for labor, equipment, vehicle maintenance and fuel. The new $482.16 assessment remains below the city's previously established maximum rate of $513.70.

The increase comes as Port St. Lucie's trash service remains a major issue for residents. The city previously reached a $24 million settlement with Waste Pro over poor service, and voters are expected to decide in November whether to bring back twice-weekly garbage pickup.

hero.body:
Christopher John Baptist was pulled over for a minor traffic violation in Vero Beach but deputies say he took off, reaching speeds more than 50 mph over the limit. The pursuit ended when Baptist crashed his vehicle and fled on foot.

 Deputies called in K9 Remy, who tracked Baptist to a nearby area and found him hiding under brush. Baptist was taken into custody and faces charges including fleeing and eluding at high speed, speeding more than 50 mph over the posted limit, providing false identification, resisting without violence, leaving the scene of a crash, driving with a suspended license, possession of a controlled substance, possession of drug paraphernalia, and felony probation violation.

 Baptist remains in custody as he faces the charges. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office shared the arrest as part of its latest enforcement updates.

cards.body:
Jabari Cowart, 36, has been charged with manslaughter after Fort Pierce police say he fatally shot a 34-year-old man with a BB gun on Saturday in the 2900 block of Avenue G near an elementary school. Police said a group of men in their 30s had been shooting a BB gun at trees when Cowart asked to use the BB gun, then pointed it at one of the men and pulled the trigger. The victim fell to the ground, and officers were called to the scene.

Ken Noble, marketing manager at The Tactical Store in Fort Pierce, said BB guns can be extremely dangerous. "It's a piece of metal moving really, really fast," Noble said. He explained that BB guns, while often considered less harmful than traditional firearms, can still cause serious injury or death.

"Anything with a projectile can be a weapon. As I stated before, anything's moving fast enough, it can penetrate skin, hit vital spots, and it can be very lethal," Noble said. He added that safety procedures are critical when handling any type of firearm, including BB guns.

Noble shared safety advice for anyone handling firearms. "You shouldn't point anything at anyone," he said. "As long as you follow safety procedures and use a little bit of sense, you ain't got anything to worry about." Fort Pierce police said Cowart is being held at the St. Lucie County jail.

cards.body:
Donalds announced the pick at Miami's Freedom Tower, a landmark closely tied to South Florida's Cuban exile community. Avila was born and raised in Hialeah after his parents fled Cuba. He now lives in Miami Springs with his wife, Cindy, and their two children. The selection gives Donalds, a Southwest Florida congressman, a running mate with deep political and personal ties to Miami-Dade and its influential Cuban-American community.

Avila was first elected to the Florida House in 2014 and eventually rose to speaker pro tempore. He won election to the Senate in 2022 and currently chairs the Finance and Tax Committee. Avila also sponsored the Stop WOKE Act, one of Gov. Ron DeSantis' signature culture-war measures. The law restricts certain instruction and training involving race, discrimination and privilege in schools and workplaces. Parts of the law have been blocked by federal courts.

Donalds and Avila will campaign on affordability, lower taxes, public safety, parental rights and school choice. They face Democratic nominee David Jolly and his running mate, former Democratic Congresswoman Gwen Graham, in the November general election. Jolly congratulated Avila on the selection but argued the race will remain centered on Donalds' close political alliance with President Donald Trump.

hero.body:
About 440,000 Floridians dropped their Affordable Care Act health insurance plans this year, more than any other state, after Congress allowed enhanced federal subsidies to expire in January. The lapse forced millions of Americans to choose between keeping coverage that often doubled or tripled in cost or going without insurance.

Florida's large population of gig workers, entrepreneurs and small business owners relies heavily on the federal health insurance marketplace, making the state one of the most visible epicenters of the impact. Elijah Button, a 21-year-old chef in St. Cloud, gave up his plan in January after a $100 monthly premium hike he could not afford. When he sliced his middle finger to the bone in June while chopping onions, he treated the injury at home with his uncle's help using a butterfly bandage, splint and daily cleanings. Thousands more Floridians who kept coverage are struggling to pay for necessities as health insurers project another year of double-digit premium hikes.

The healthcare cost crisis has become a major campaign issue in the deep-red state where congressional districts were recently redrawn to strongly favor Republicans. Republican midterm candidates have been promoting fraud crackdowns to protect federal health programs, while Democrats have been urging voters to help Congress change hands so they can restore subsidies. Lawmakers have taken no action to replace the lost federal funds.

Button said the scar from his injury gnaws at him as a symbol of what else could go wrong without health insurance. Some Floridians are dealing with strained budgets and exorbitant medical bills, while others avoid the doctor in fear of the cost. Prices of necessities like groceries and gasoline remain steep, compounding the financial pressure on families across the state.
hero.headline: Florida leads nation in Affordable Care Act coverage losses as 440,000 drop health plans amid subsidy expiration

hero.body:
About 440,000 Floridians dropped their Affordable Care Act health insurance plans this year after enhanced federal subsidies expired in January, more than in any other state, according to figures first reported by The Associated Press. Residents who lost coverage are now skipping medical care or facing mounting debt as premiums continue climbing with no action from Congress to replace the lost funds. Florida's large population of gig workers, entrepreneurs and small business owners relies heavily on the federal health insurance marketplace, making the state one of the most visible epicenters of the impact from the subsidy expiration.

Elijah Button, a 21-year-old chef in St. Cloud, gave up his Affordable Care Act plan in January after a $100 monthly premium hike he could not afford. When he sliced his middle finger to the bone while chopping onions in June, he did not seek emergency care. Button instead asked his uncle for help, and the wound healed with a butterfly bandage, splint and daily cleanings and dressings. The scar remains a reminder of what else could go wrong without insurance coverage.

Millions of Americans faced the decision of whether to keep insurance that often doubled or tripled in cost or go without coverage after Republicans in Congress let the enhanced subsidies expire. Thousands of Floridians who kept their plans are struggling to afford them as prices of groceries and gasoline remain high and health insurers project another year of double-digit premium hikes. The struggles in Florida reflect broader nationwide concerns over rising healthcare costs and a lack of meaningful policy to address them.

Healthcare costs have become a major campaign issue in Florida, where congressional districts were recently redrawn to strongly favor Republicans. Republican midterm candidates have been promoting fraud crackdowns to protect federal health programs, while Democrats have been urging voters to help Congress change hands so they can restore subsidies. Button is estranged from his parents and lives with his aunt and uncle in their suburban home.

cards.body:
Ronald Corbin, who taught choral music at Martin County High School in Stuart for 34 years, died Saturday. Corbin led OPUS, which stands for Outstanding People United to Sing, from 1980 until his retirement in 2014. He began his teaching career at Bartow High School in Polk County before coming to the Stuart school.

The Martin County School District posted on Instagram that Corbin dedicated his career to helping students find their voices and discover the joy of music. All 36 Border Collies removed from a Palm City home on Southwest Alligator Street earlier this month have been legally surrendered to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. The dogs were rescued Aug. 10 from a home where investigators found them living without air conditioning and surrounded by feces, urine-soaked materials and debris. Many arrived at the shelter dirty, severely matted and covered in dried waste.

Paige ODonnell, 62, was arrested in the case and faces 72 charges including 36 third-degree felony counts of animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. Her bond was set at $270,000, and a judge ordered that she not have pets if released. Shelter staff have removed the dogs matted fur and cleaned away the layers of dried feces as the animals begin their recovery.

The Humane Society will complete medical testing and behavioral evaluations so potential adopters have clear information about each dogs needs. The dogs will be spayed or neutered, microchipped and vaccinated on a phased schedule. Adoption applications for the Border Collies, including applications from nonprofit rescue groups, will be available beginning Sept. 1 through the Humane Societys website and Facebook page.

Adoption fees will be $140 for adult Border Collies and $175 for puppies. The shelter said applicants will be carefully screened to find appropriate placements. The shelter is asking people not to call about the dogs so its phone lines remain available for urgent needs. While it does not need pet food or supplies at this time, it is accepting donations to its Emergency Medical Fund to help cover veterinary care for the Border Collies and other shelter animals.

An EF0 tornado touched down in Port St. Lucie Sunday evening with maximum estimated wind gusts between 65 and 75 mph, according to the National Weather Service. The tornado traveled 2.1 miles and also moved over the St. Lucie River, where it was seen as a waterspout.

The tornado began at 6:10 p.m. near SE Kitchen Cove Lane and SE Morningside Boulevard and ended near SE Quay Street and SE Cody Place. The maximum width of the tornado was 200 yards.

Viewers submitted photos and videos of apparent funnel clouds in the sky from Port St. Lucie, Jensen Beach and Palm City.

Residents near Southbend Boulevard and Southeast Navy Ave in Port St. Lucie are cleaning up after a possible tornado or landspout hit their neighborhood Sunday. Aaron Christiansen said he was home around 6 p.m. when he noticed dark clouds and debris through his window and had about 10 seconds to take cover with his dogs before the storm hit.

Christiansen found significant damage in his backyard after the storm. His patio furniture was submerged in his pool, his pool fence was blown toward his home, debris was scattered across the ground and plants were blown away. Christiansen and his family and pets were not injured.

Christiansen, originally from Minnesota, said his experience with tornado-like weather helped him know what precautions to take. He said he received the emergency alert after the storm had already hit. Christiansen said he plans to begin cleanup efforts Monday and will have his roof inspected.

hero.body:
Jabari Cowart, 36, has been charged with manslaughter after Fort Pierce police say he fatally shot a 34-year-old man with a BB gun on Saturday near an elementary school. Police said the incident happened in the 2900 block of Avenue G, where a group of men in their 30s had been shooting a BB gun at trees. Investigators believe Cowart asked to use the BB gun and later pointed it at one of the men before pulling the trigger. The victim fell to the ground, and officers were called to the scene.

Ken Noble, marketing manager at The Tactical Store in Fort Pierce, said BB guns can be extremely dangerous. "It's a piece of metal moving really, really fast," Noble said. He explained that BB guns, while often considered less harmful than traditional firearms, can still cause serious injury or death. "Anything with a projectile can be a weapon. As I stated before, anything's moving fast enough, it can penetrate skin, hit vital spots, and it can be very lethal," Noble said.

Noble shared safety advice for handling firearms, including BB guns. "You shouldn't point anything at anyone," he said. "As long as you follow safety procedures and use a little bit of sense, you ain't got anything to worry about." Fort Pierce police said Cowart is being held at the St. Lucie County jail.

hero.body:
Port St. Lucie residents will pay $482.16 annually for trash service beginning in October after the City Council approved a $14.83 increase Monday night. The council approved Resolution 26-R70, raising the annual solid waste assessment from $467.33 per dwelling unit for the fiscal year beginning in October. There was no public comment or council discussion before the item was read and approved.

The assessment pays for garbage collection, disposal services, facilities and related solid waste programs. It is collected through residents' property tax bills. The increase amounts to about $1.24 more per month for residential properties. City officials previously said the increase is required under Port St. Lucie's solid waste franchise agreement with FCC Environmental Service and reflects rising costs for labor, equipment, vehicle maintenance and fuel.

The new $482.16 assessment remains below the city's previously established maximum rate of $513.70. The increase comes as Port St. Lucie's trash service remains a major issue for residents. The city previously reached a $24 million settlement with Waste Pro over poor service.

Voters are expected to decide in November whether to bring back twice-weekly garbage pickup. The referendum follows persistent complaints about trash collection service quality in the city.
hero.headline: Port St. Lucie approves higher annual trash fee despite ongoing service complaints

shadow.final_hero_headline: Vero Beach man crashes while fleeing deputies, K9 finds him hiding under brush

hero.angle: Vero Beach man faces multiple felony and misdemeanor charges after leading Indian River County deputies on a high-speed chase, crashing, and being tracked down by K9 unit while hiding in brush.

cards.body:
Christopher John Baptist was pulled over for a minor traffic violation in Vero Beach but deputies say he took off, reaching speeds more than 50 mph over the limit. The pursuit ended when Baptist crashed his vehicle and fled on foot.

 Deputies called in K9 Remy, who tracked Baptist to a nearby area and found him hiding under brush. Baptist was taken into custody and faces charges including fleeing and eluding at high speed, speeding more than 50 mph over the posted limit, providing false identification, resisting without violence, leaving the scene of a crash, driving with a suspended license, possession of a controlled substance, possession of drug paraphernalia, and felony probation violation.

 Baptist remains in custody as he faces the charges. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office shared the arrest as part of its latest enforcement updates.

hero.body:
A Vero Beach man is facing multiple felony and misdemeanor charges after leading Indian River County deputies on a high-speed chase that ended in a crash and foot pursuit. Christopher John Baptist was arrested after K9 Remy tracked him down hiding under brush following the Monday incident.

Baptist was initially pulled over for a minor traffic violation but fled the traffic stop, reaching speeds more than 50 mph over the limit, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office. The pursuit ended when Baptist crashed his vehicle and fled on foot.

Deputies called in K9 Remy, who tracked Baptist to a nearby area and found him hiding under brush. Baptist was taken into custody at the scene.

Baptist faces charges including fleeing and eluding at high speed, speeding more than 50 mph over the posted limit, providing false identification, resisting without violence, leaving the scene of a crash, driving with a suspended license, possession of a controlled substance, possession of drug paraphernalia, and felony probation violation. The sheriff's office shared the arrest as part of its latest enforcement updates. Baptist remains in custody as he faces the charges.
